**Answer – where the phrase actually comes from**

| Source | Verse / Text | Key Words |
|--------|--------------|-----------|
| **Bible – King James Version (KJV)** | **Job 19:20** | “I have escaped with the **skin of my teeth**.” |
| (Also numbered Job 20:20 in some modern/modern‑numbered Bibles) | “I escaped by the skin of my teeth.” | |

- The phrase *“by the skin of your teeth”* is a transliteration of the Hebrew phrase **הַיָּברָה אֶל הֶרְטַד (hayyībā ʾel hertad)**, meaning “I was saved by the smallest safe space”, i.e. by the narrowest margin.
- The earliest English translations that render the idea literally are the **Geneva Bible (1560)** and the **Wycliffe Bible (1382‑88)**. In the modern KJV it appears exactly in Job 19:20.

**Why no Mary is mentioned**

The verse that gives the idiom (Job 19:20) contains no reference to any person named Mary (Figures of Mary in the Bible such as the Virgin‑Mary appear in the Gospels—Matthew 1:18, Mark 1:45, Luke 1:26, John 19:25‑27, etc. – but the phrase “skin of the teeth” is not among them).

**How to cite it**

If you want a formal reference for the idiom you can cite:

- *Job 19:20* (KJV) – “I have escaped with the skin of my teeth.”
- *Job 20:20* (KJV) – in other chapter‑verses it appears as Job 20:20.

> **Note:** Modern Bibles that follow the 1611 *New King James* or *New King James* and many modern incisions might number the verse as *Job 20:20*, but the wording is the same. The exact verse is the **source** for the idiom “by the skin of your teeth.”

**Bottom line**

- The idiom “by the skin of your teeth” comes *solely* from the biblical book of **Job**, verse 19:20 (or 20:20 in some modern chapter‑verses).  
- The phrase is **not** associated with any Mary in Scripture. If you need references to Mary, consult the Gospels (Matthew 1, Mark 1, Luke 1, John 19, etc.).
